title: Atomic Commits and git commit --amend
learning_objectives: Define an atomic commit and explain why it matters for project history
Recognize commits that mix concerns and know how to avoid them
Use git commit --amend to fix message mistakes before pushing
Understand the 'before pushing' rule for amend and why it exists
Apply atomic commit discipline to Helm development
outline: What is an atomic commit: one logical change, one commit
Why atomic commits matter: bisect, revert, code review, blame
Anti-patterns: mixing a bug fix with a refactor in one commit
Practical strategies: stage selectively with git add -p
git commit --amend: fixing a message before it's pushed
The golden rule: never amend a commit that others have pulled
Hands-on: Use --amend to fix a bad commit message in the Helm repo

helm_context.feature: Clean, reviewable commit history for Helm
helm_context.deliverable: A corrected commit in the Helm repo using git commit --amend

criteria: Can articulate what makes a commit 'atomic' in their own words
Successfully uses git commit --amend to fix a message
Understands and can state when amend is and isn't safe to use
Demonstrates git add -p or shows awareness of selective staging

professor_constraints: Use Helm-specific examples for atomic commit scenarios (task model change vs. UI styling)
Be explicit about the 'before pushing' safety rule for --amend — this is a common mistake
Keep the hands-on exercise simple: one intentionally bad commit to fix with --amend
Mention git add -p briefly but don't deep-dive — it comes back in later phases
